reviews.title: $22 a week not $22 a month
reviews.text: My 89-year-old mother was duped into paying $22 a month for this overpriced app. I canceled her subscription, and she removed her credit card from her Apple account. Later, she decided to add the card back, and IQ Boost immediately charged her checking account another $22. They are just waiting to prey on people. EDIT: it was not $22 a month. It was $22 a week. Run, don’t walk away from downloading this app.

reviews.title: Deceiving
reviews.text:
Verdict: Not effective at what it claims — and it shows several red flags.

On its claims: The app promises to “improve IQ” via “scientifically-designed” training, but it cites no studies, has no research backing, and its core claim contradicts the scientific consensus. Large studies (including one in Nature with 11,000+ participants) and a 70-scientist Stanford/Max Planck consensus statement show brain games make you better at the games themselves, not at IQ or everyday cognition. The FTC even fined Lumosity $2M for making milder versions of these exact claims.

Red flags specific to this app:

	•	Weekly subscriptions listed from $9.99 up to $89.99/week (that’s ~$4,600/year) with inconsistent duplicate tiers — a hallmark of aggressive price testing
	•	Reviews report broken games, a $3.99 purchase that charged $64, ads after every level, and nearly everything paywalled
	•	Single individual developer account, 2025 release, privacy policy on a free Google Sites page, and location data used to track you across apps
